reason: The sources support 20 cross-verified claims across independent sites detailing the history and observational receipts of the expanding universe.
story:
In 1927, Belgian physicist and Catholic priest Georges Lemaitre made an astounding realization: Albert Einstein's equations showed the universe was expanding, not static. Two years later at Mount Wilson, Edwin Hubble observed distant galaxies speeding away, confirming Lemaitre's mathematical deductions. Tracing this motion backward in time, Lemaitre reasoned that all matter originally resided inside an unimaginably dense primordial atom.

For decades, many astronomers rejected the idea, preferring an eternal, unchanging steady-state universe. That debate collapsed in 1964 when Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson accidentally detected the cosmic microwave background—ancient relic light freed when the cooling cosmos turned transparent roughly 380,000 years after the start.

Subsequent space observatories confirmed the universe underwent dramatic inflation during its first split second, seeding future galaxies from quantum fluctuations. Even stranger, ordinary stars and planets make up less than five percent of the cosmos, leaving the rest to invisible dark matter and dark energy.
angle: The Big Bang theory was not conceived by an army of modern astrophysicists, but in 1927 by a Belgian Catholic priest who proved Einstein's static universe was wrong.

claims.claim: Georges Lemaitre, who formulated the expanding universe model, was a Belgian Catholic priest and physicist.
In 1927, Lemaitre proposed that astronomical redshifts were caused by the physical expansion of the universe.
Alexander Friedmann independently derived expanding universe solutions from Einstein's equations prior to Lemaitre.
In 1929, Edwin Hubble published observations proving that galaxies are moving away from Earth at high velocities.
Hubble made his key galactic observations using the 100-inch telescope at Mount Wilson Observatory in California.
Lemaitre proposed that running cosmic expansion backward led to a primordial atom containing all matter in the universe.
The expanding model competed for decades against the steady-state theory, which claimed the universe was eternal and unchanging.
In 1964, Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson discovered the cosmic microwave background radiation.
The discovery of cosmic microwave background radiation effectively settled the debate against the steady-state model.
Before recombination, the early universe was filled with an opaque hot plasma that trapped light.
The cosmic microwave background was released roughly 370,000 to 380,000 years after the Big Bang when the universe cooled and became transparent.
Cosmic inflation was an extremely brief phase of accelerated, dramatic expansion in the universe's earliest moments.
Microscopic quantum fluctuations in the infant universe served as the seeds that gravitationally grew into stars and galaxies.
Normal baryonic matter makes up only about 4.6 to 5 percent of the universe's total mass-energy density.
Dark energy accounts for the largest fraction of the universe's total energy density, roughly 68 to 73 percent.
Dark matter does not interact with light and is detected through its gravitational influence on visible matter.
Leaders of the Cosmic Background Explorer (COBE) satellite team were awarded the 2006 Nobel Prize in Physics.
Detecting primordial gravitational waves could provide direct observational relics from the first moments of the Big Bang.
Observations of temperature variations in the cosmic microwave background show that the geometry of the universe is close to spatially flat.
NASA's Wilkinson Microwave Anisotropy Probe (WMAP) scanned the entire sky to produce high-precision maps of relic radiation.

disputed: Whether the Big Bang was an 'explosion': S2 and S7 describe the Big Bang as an explosion of a primordial atom bursting outward, whereas S1 emphasizes that treating it as an explosion into empty space is a scientific misnomer, as general relativity describes the expansion of space itself. A script should leave out 'explosion' when explaining the physics or clarify that 'explosion' was an early informal description.

Fred Hoyle's motive in coining 'Big Bang': S1 and S2 note popular reports that astronomer Fred Hoyle coined the phrase during a 1949 BBC broadcast to mock the theory, but Hoyle explicitly denied this, saying it was merely a vivid metaphor. A script should attribute this cautiously: 'According to popular lore, Hoyle meant it as an insult, though he claimed it was just a vivid comparison.'
